query: For W–Cu metal-matrix composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, what single intervention could increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite, defines the application conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a thin, conformal nickel interlayer at the tungsten–copper interfaces will reduce interfacial thermal resistance, thereby increasing the overall thermal conductivity of the composite while maintaining its mechanical durability and irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional W–Cu composite fabricated via standard processing, in which the W and Cu phases are bonded directly, leading to relatively high interfacial thermal resistance.
generation.intervention: Introduce a nanoscale, uniform nickel coating on tungsten surfaces (or at the W–Cu interface) via methods such as physical vapor deposition or electroless plating prior to composite consolidation.
generation.conditions: The composite is subjected to the temperature ranges and irradiation environments typical of fusion-reactor joint or heat-dissipation applications (i.e., high heat flux and moderate to high neutron flux conditions).
generation.structural_mediator: An engineered, continuous nickel interlayer that enhances interfacial bonding between tungsten and copper, thereby reducing phonon/electron scattering at the interface.
generation.mechanism: The Ni interlayer promotes better lattice coupling between tungsten and copper, minimizing the thermal boundary resistance that typically limits electron and phonon transport. Its presence also acts as a diffusion barrier during processing and under irradiation, helping maintain mechanical integrity and delaying the formation of irradiation-induced defects.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified composite will show a notably higher effective thermal conductivity compared to a standard W–Cu composite, while retaining similar levels of mechanical strength and irradiation resistance.
generation.baseline: W–Cu composites produced without the nickel interlayer.
generation.boundary: The benefit is expected when the primary limitation is interfacial thermal resistance; if the Ni coating is non-uniform or excessively thick, it may compromise the intended improvements. Furthermore, the long-term performance under extreme irradiation may require additional validation.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal thickness and deposition method for the nickel interlayer need to be determined, and its behavior over extended irradiation cycles is not fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composites: one set incorporating the engineered nanoscale nickel interlayer and one set prepared by conventional means. Expose both sets to simulated fusion-relevant operational conditions including high heat flux and neutron irradiation. Perform comparative testing on thermal conductivity, mechanical durability (e.g., tensile, fatigue tests), and microstructural stability post-irradiation.
measurements: Effective thermal conductivity (e.g., via laser flash analysis)
Mechanical performance metrics (e.g., yield strength, fracture toughness)
Microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM for defect analysis, interface integrity)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the composites with the nickel interlayer do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., >10% increase) in thermal conductivity under operating conditions, or if they show degraded mechanical durability or irradiation resistance relative to the baseline composites, the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this context, one of the biggest challenges is the development of structural and functional materials that can withstand the conditions inside the reactor: high temperature, high heat flux, and intense flux of high energy neutrons []. The diverter, located at the bottom of the plasma chamber, where the thermal power from the plasma is exhausted [], is one of the most challenging areas. Tungsten (W), with a high melting temperature, low sputtering rates, low neutron activation, and low tritium and deuterium retention [,], was chosen as the plasma-facing material. CuCrZr alloy was chosen as the heat sink due to its high thermal conductivity and strength. However, there is a gap between the operating temperatures of these two materials. Tungsten presents a high ductile–brittle temperature transition (DBTT) [], which requires a high-temperature operation, while CuCrZr alloy presents relatively low working temperatures (180–350 °C) [], with loss of ductility caused by irradiation embrittlement at lower temperatures and loss of mechanical strength at higher temperatures due to over-aging [,].
